narrative:
The model determined that you have a 91.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess risk, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by your academic performance during law school. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the two strongest factors pushing the model toward predicting failure. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your class—far below the average of roughly the 6th decile among students who were accepted. These unusually low rankings signaled to the model a pattern of academic struggle that strongly outweighed other information.

Your LSAT score was the third most important factor, but it worked mildly in your favor. At 37, it sits almost exactly at the average of accepted students, giving the model a small reason to expect you might pass.

Everything else about your profile—your upper-middle family income, 3.10 undergraduate GPA, full-time status, gender, and race—played only minor roles. The model focused overwhelmingly on your law-school grades.

To improve your chances, you should consider retaking key courses, seeking academic support, or gaining additional legal experience before reapplying. Strengthening your academic record will be the most direct way to shift future predictions in your favor. (218 words)
